p: The 'ezor was a wrap worn next to the skin, and linen was priestly cloth.
b: The Hebrew 'ezor is a cloth wrapped around the hips and held in place by its own folds, an undergarment rather than a belt (the KJV 'girdle' suggests a belt). It was made of linen, the cloth of priests (Exodus 28:42; Leviticus 16:4; Ezekiel 44:17-18). Jeremiah was a priest's son (1:1), so the sign may touch his own family's clothing. The command not to wash it matters: the cloth must go to its hiding place and come back in the state it was in, so its ruin comes from the place and the time, not from laundering.

p: Perath is the usual Hebrew name of the Euphrates, but a town called Parah lay near Anathoth.
b: Perath is the ordinary Hebrew name of the Euphrates (Genesis 2:14), and the Greek translator wrote 'Euphrates' here. Readers divide in three. (1) Jeremiah made the journey, hundreds of miles each way, twice, and the distance is part of the sign: the cloth is hidden in the river of Babylon, the place of the coming exile. (2) He did not travel; it was a vision or a told parable, a view held by many commentators, ancient and modern. (3) The word means Parah (Joshua 18:23), a Benjamite town a few miles from Anathoth with a spring in the Wadi Farah, and the sign is a short walk from home; the long journey was then an old misreading of the name. The text itself does not say which, and the sign works under all three: the cloth rots in a place the LORD chose. See Lundbom and Thompson for the discussion.

a: my people, my name, my praise and my honor
t: Israel as the LORD's name and praise
p: The four words come from the promise of Deuteronomy 26:19.
b: The LORD's purpose for Israel is stated in four nouns: a people, a name, a praise and an honor. The last three echo the promise of Deuteronomy 26:19, that the LORD would set Israel high above the nations in praise, name and splendor (the Hebrew words are tehillah, shem, tiferet). Jeremiah 33:9 uses the same set for the restored Jerusalem. The loincloth that clung to the hips is meant to be the kind of garment that is never taken off, and a garment that is both worn close and worn out is a picture of a people who were meant to adorn God and instead were spoiled.

p: The verb is the one Deuteronomy uses for holding fast to God.
b: The loincloth 'clings' (davaq) to the body, and the LORD made Israel 'cling' (hidbaqti) to himself. The verb is the one Deuteronomy uses for holding on to God (Deuteronomy 10:20; 11:22; 13:4) and Genesis 2:24 uses for a husband clinging to his wife. Here it is the LORD who does the joining, as he did at the Exodus, and the people who are 'good for nothing' because they did not hold. The image is close and bodily, like the marriage pictures of 2:2 and 3:1-5.

a: Every jar will be filled with wine
p: The word nevel can mean a pottery jar or a skin bag; the smashing in verse 14 fits a pot.
b: The word nevel names a large container for wine. It can be a skin bottle, as the Greek translator took it (askos), but in most places it is a pottery jar (Lamentations 4:2; Isaiah 30:14 uses the same word in a figure of a jar smashed). The Plain English Translation says 'jar' because verse 14 has the LORD smash people 'against one another', as jars are smashed. The saying itself may be a toast or a proverb, so obvious that the people reply 'Do we not know?' Jeremiah then makes the obvious saying a threat: they will be filled with the LORD's anger. The Plain English Translation does not decide whether the people took it as a blessing or a boast.

t: The cup of the LORD's anger
p: Drunkenness is a standing picture in the prophets for what judgment does to a people.
b: A people staggering and helpless under judgment is drunk with the LORD's anger. Jeremiah returns to it in the cup of 25:15-29 and the golden cup of Babylon in 51:7; Isaiah 51:17-23 and Psalm 75:8 use it too. Revelation 14:10 and 16:19 draw on the same tradition. In 13:13 the drunk include the kings 'who sit on David's throne', the priests and the prophets, the three groups the book keeps accusing (2:8, 26). The smashing of jars in verse 14 shows the result: drunk men fall on each other.

t: Deep shadow, or the shadow of death?
p: Tsalmavet is the word of Psalm 23; most now read it as 'deep shadow'.
b: The word tsalmavet is traditionally read as 'shadow of death' (tsel 'shadow' plus mavet 'death'; Psalm 23:4 in the KJV). Many modern scholars take it as a rare word for deep darkness, a compound that only looks like 'death' (the Plain English Translation follows the second reading, as in Job). Either way the picture is of travelers caught in the dark on the mountain paths at twilight. Jeremiah says the LORD himself brings the dark, as he promised to bring the light in Isaiah 9:2.

a: my whole self will weep in secret places
p: The weeper is called 'I' and speaks of 'the LORD's flock' in the third person.
b: Tradition calls Jeremiah 'the weeping prophet', and 9:1 and 14:17 give him tears. Here the speaker says 'my eye' yet speaks of 'the LORD's flock', which is how a prophet would speak. Some interpreters hold that in these laments the voices of the prophet and of God run together, so that Jeremiah's grief is also the LORD's (so Fretheim). Others hold that the weeper is always the prophet, who feels the people's pain and shares the LORD's sorrow (so Heschel's idea of the prophet's 'pathos', the feeling he shares with God). Either way, the book wants its readers to see that the judgment does not please the one who announces it.

t: A kingdom closed in from the south
p: The Negev towns are shut, and no one can open them.
b: The Negev is the dry south of Judah. 'Shut up' may mean sealed off by siege, or blocked so that no help can pass. After the first Babylonian capture of Jerusalem in 597 BC, King Jehoiachin, his mother and the leading men were taken to Babylon (2 Kings 24:10-16), which fits verses 18-19: the royal house has lost its crown, and Judah is carried off 'completely'. Some commentators put the poem a little earlier or later, in the years of Babylon's pressure after 605, and the Plain English Translation leaves it open.

p: The written text addresses Jerusalem; the Masoretes marked it to be read as plural.
b: The command to look at the foe from the north is written in the feminine singular (a city, here Jerusalem; so also the Greek, which adds 'Jerusalem'), but a note in the margin says to read it as a plural, as if the whole people were being addressed (the Ketiv and Qere of the Masoretic Text). The verses that follow ('your sheep', 'you taught') are feminine singular, so the Plain English Translation follows the written form. English 'your eyes' hides the difference; it matters only for who is being scolded. 4QJer-a does not preserve this verse.

a: the friends you yourself taught to be close to you
p: The Hebrew is rough; the likely sense is that Judah trained its own future masters.
b: The Hebrew of this verse is crowded and broken, and the translations differ widely. The Plain English Translation follows the most natural reading of the words in order: God will 'appoint over you' as 'head' the very ones Judah 'taught' (or trained) to be its close friends. The likeliest case is the alliance with Babylon, for which Hezekiah's showing his treasure to Merodach-baladan's envoys is the ancestor (2 Kings 20:12-19; Isaiah 39); Judah's partners will become its rulers. The Greek takes the line quite differently ('you taught them lessons against you, for rule'), and the pains of a woman in labor close the verse as in 4:31 and 6:24.

t: Exposure as punishment, and why modern readers object
p: Prophets use a woman's public exposure as a picture of a city's shame.
b: Lifting a woman's skirts, stripping her and shaming her in public was a punishment in Israelite and Near Eastern law and a picture of a conquered city (Hosea 2:10; Nahum 3:5; Isaiah 47:2-3; Ezekiel 16:37; Lamentations 1:8-9). 'Heels' may mean the feet and legs of a stripped captive woman, or may be a polite word for a sexual assault. Here and in 13:26 the picture is a threat of what armies do to the women of a conquered city. Many modern readers object that the prophets blame a woman for her own abuse. The text's own point is that the LORD allows what the people's choices have invited. The reader will want to hold the objection and the text side by side.

a: Can a Cushite change his skin
t: Cush is not modern Ethiopia, and the saying is about habit
p: A Cushite was a person from Nubia, south of Egypt; the point is how hard it is to change a settled nature.
b: Cush is the land south of Egypt along the Nile (Nubia, in what is now Sudan). The KJV 'Ethiopian' follows the Greek Aithiops, which meant a dark-skinned person in Greek and was not the modern country. The saying joins two things that cannot change, a skin color and the spots of a leopard, to make a point about people who are 'trained in doing evil': habit has become nature. It is a saying about the difficulty of turning, not about a race, and it has sometimes been misused. Elsewhere Jeremiah says the LORD can write the law on the heart (31:33). Ebed-melech, who saves Jeremiah, is called a Cushite in 38:7.

p: Sheqer is Jeremiah's word for what is false and so cannot hold weight.
b: Sheqer is one of the book's chief words. It covers lies, false oaths, false prophecy, false religion and whatever cannot bear the weight put on it. The temple is 'falsehood' (7:4), the scribes' pen produces it (8:8), the prophets speak it (14:14; 23:25), and the idols are the ancestors' inheritance of it (16:19). To 'trust in falsehood' is to lean on something that gives way. Here it follows 'you forgot me', as 2:32 and 3:21 also say of Israel. The Plain English Translation says 'falsehood' wherever the word has this wide sense, 'lie' where a person speaks it.

t: Idolatry as adultery, and a stallion's neigh
p: Judah's worship on the hills is pictured as lust.
b: Hosea began the prophets' picture of idolatry as adultery (Hosea 1-3), and Jeremiah carries it on (2:20; 3:2, 6-9). 'Neighing' compares the people to horses in heat; 5:8 uses the same picture of stallions after other men's wives. The 'hills in the field' are the high places where other gods were worshiped. The picture is of the whole people, not only a few; and it ends in the cry 'Woe to you, Jerusalem', and a question with no answer: how long?

p: The drought is a punishment named in the covenant, and the poem is built as a liturgy.
b: Lack of rain was one of the curses written into the covenant (Leviticus 26:19-20; Deuteronomy 11:13-17; 28:23-24), and Elijah's drought had shown the LORD controlling the rain against Baal (1 Kings 17-18). The heading uses the plural 'droughts' (batstsorot), perhaps for a series of dry years; 17:8 has the singular, 'a year of drought'. The chapter then moves in the order of a communal lament: a description of the disaster (14:2-6), the people's prayer (7-9), the LORD's refusal (10-12), a complaint about false prophets (13-16), and a second prayer (19-22). The date is not given, and the drought cannot be tied to a year.
r: Leviticus 26:19-20; Deuteronomy 11:13-17; Deuteronomy 28:23-24; 1 Kings 17:1; Jeremiah 3:3; Jeremiah 12:4

p: In 2:13 Israel dug broken cisterns; now the cisterns are dry.
b: In 2:13 the LORD charged Israel with leaving 'the spring of living water' and digging cisterns that cannot hold water. In the drought the cisterns are empty, and the nobles' servants return with empty jars, 'ashamed and humiliated'. The cistern also becomes a prison for Jeremiah in 38:6. The detail of covering the head is a sign of grief and shame (2 Samuel 15:30; Esther 6:12).

p: Jeremiah's great pun on shuv, 'turn', is in the people's own confession.
b: The word is meshuvot, from shuv, 'turn', Jeremiah's most important verb. The same root says 'turn back' (repent) and 'turn away' (apostasy), and Jeremiah plays on both again and again (3:12, 14, 22; 8:4-5). The KJV 'backslidings' is this word. The people confess that their 'turnings' are many. The LORD's answer in 15:19 uses the same verb in the opposite direction: 'If you turn back, I will turn you back.'

t: Hope, or a pool of water?
p: Miqveh means 'hope' and also 'a gathering of water', and this is a chapter about water.
b: The word miqveh can mean 'hope', from qavah 'wait', or 'a gathering of water, a pool' (Genesis 1:10). In a chapter about empty cisterns the double meaning is hard to miss, and 17:13 makes it plain: 'O hope of Israel, LORD ... the spring of living water.' The prayer's sense is 'you in whom Israel hopes', but the hearers could also have heard 'you, Israel's pool'. The prayer then complains that God is like a foreigner or traveler, someone passing through who stays only for a night.

p: Niddam is found only here; the Greek has 'sleeping'.
b: The Hebrew niddam occurs only here, and its sense is a guess from the context. 'Astounded' or 'stunned' suits the parallel with a warrior who cannot save. The Greek has 'sleeping', which would fit a Hebrew word nirdam (the verb of Jonah 1:5-6, where Jonah is asleep); whether the Greek translator read a different word or simply guessed is not certain. God asleep is a charge the psalms make (Psalm 44:23).

p: The LORD quotes a threat from Hosea almost word for word.
b: The last two lines are almost the same as Hosea 8:13 ('he will remember their guilt and punish their sins'), also said of a people that loved sacrifices and wandering (Hosea 8:13; 9:9). Jeremiah is plainly quoting or sharing a saying of the northern prophet. The opposite is the promise of the new covenant, where the LORD says 'I will remember their sin no more' (31:34). The Plain English Translation keeps the shift from 'I' to 'the LORD ... he' that the Hebrew has.

a: Do not pray for the good of this people
p: Jeremiah is told three times not to pray for the people.
b: Moses, Samuel and Amos all prayed and were heard or came close (Exodus 32:11-14; 1 Samuel 12:19-23; Amos 7:1-6), but Jeremiah is told, here and in 7:16 and 11:14, to stop. The ban comes after he has prayed (14:7-9, 19-22), which makes it a verdict and not a rebuke (the prayers of 14:7-9 and 14:19-22 are spoken by 'the people', or perhaps by Jeremiah for them). Yet later kings still ask for his prayer (37:3; 42:2), and his letter tells the exiles to pray for Babylon's welfare (29:7). The ban tells the hearers that the time for turning aside the judgment has passed; it does not say prayer is wrong.
r: Jeremiah 7:16; Jeremiah 11:14; Jeremiah 15:1; Jeremiah 37:3; Jeremiah 42:2; Exodus 32:11-14

a: burnt offering and a grain offering
t: Fasts and offerings the LORD will not take
p: Jeremiah joins the prophets who say worship without turning back is empty.
b: The people fast in the drought and bring offerings, and the LORD will take neither. The same rejection is in Isaiah 1:11-15, Hosea 6:6, Amos 5:21-22 and Micah 6:6-8, and Jeremiah has said it already (6:20; 7:21-22). The prophets are not against sacrifice as such; the message is that the rite does not replace turning back. Zechariah 7:5 asks whether the exile fasts were ever for the LORD. The verse lists the three famous scourges, sword, famine and disease, that run through the book (21:7, 9; 24:10; 27:8; 29:17).
r: Isaiah 1:11-15; Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21-22; Jeremiah 6:20; Jeremiah 7:21-22; Zechariah 7:5

p: The prophets promise 'peace of truth', and the Greek says 'truth and peace'.
b: The false prophets promise shalom 'emet, literally 'peace of truth', that is, peace that holds. The Greek reads 'truth and peace'. It is the promise Jeremiah calls a lie in 6:14, 8:11 ('Peace, peace', when there is no peace) and 23:17, and Hananiah makes in chapter 28. The point is not that peace is bad, but that these prophets promise it without a call to turn. Deuteronomy 18:21-22 gave the test: wait and see whether it happens.

t: The test of a true prophet
p: A prophet who was not sent speaks his own heart, whatever name he uses.
b: 'I did not send them' with 'I gave them no command' (tsivvah, 'command', the verb of Deuteronomy 18:20) is the charge of Deuteronomy 18:20 (a prophet who speaks 'what I did not command him') and Jeremiah's refrain about the prophets: 23:21, 32; 28:15; 29:9. The LORD lists what these men offer: a false vision, divination (the practice Deuteronomy 18:10-14 forbids), 'a worthless idol' and 'the deceit of their own hearts'. They prophesy 'in my name', so the test cannot be the name used; it has to be the sending, the message, and the outcome (Deuteronomy 18:21-22; Jeremiah 28:8-9).
r: Deuteronomy 18:10-14; Deuteronomy 18:20-22; Jeremiah 23:21; Jeremiah 23:32; Jeremiah 28:15; Jeremiah 29:9

p: The Masoretes marked the written word 'worthlessness' to be read 'idol'.
b: The consonants spell 'elul, 'worthlessness'; the Masoretes' margin says to read 'elil, 'a nothing, an idol' (the word of 'worthless idols' in the Plain English Translation). The meaning is close either way: a prophet's message that is empty. The note is placed here only so the reader sees that the printed Hebrew text and the Masoretic reading differ in one letter.

p: Literally 'the virgin daughter of my people'; the Plain English Translation says 'my dear people'.
b: The Hebrew is betulat bat 'ammi, 'the virgin daughter of my people', a way of speaking of a people as a young woman who is loved and untouched until now. Like 'Daughter Zion', the 'daughter' is not a separate person: it is the people, personified. Jeremiah uses the phrase for his tears (8:21; 9:1) and the grief is both his and, in some readings, the LORD's (see 13:17). The word 'virgin' stresses what a pity it is that she is broken.

t: Roam, trade, or go into exile?
p: The verb sakhar can mean 'go about' or 'trade'.
b: The verb sakhar is uncertain. It can mean 'travel around, go about' (the sense that suits the verse as exile or wandering) or 'trade, do business' (so some translators have prophet and priest 'plying their trade in a land they do not know'). The Greek says they 'went into a land they did not know', that is, into exile. The Plain English Translation's 'roam' keeps the wandering and leaves the cause open: prophet and priest, who were to guide the people, no longer know where they are.

p: The question is repeated in the laments of Psalms and Lamentations.
b: The question 'Have you rejected Judah?' is the question of the community laments (Psalm 44:9, 23; 74:1; 89:38) and of the end of Lamentations (5:22). The last two lines of verse 19 repeat 8:15 word for word in the Hebrew, a repeated saying: the hope for peace and a time of healing, and then terror. The people ask the questions, and the LORD's answer is the silence that follows in chapter 15.

p: The people ask God to remember a covenant they have broken.
b: To 'remember' the covenant is to act on it; the prayer repeats Moses' appeals (Exodus 32:13; Deuteronomy 9:27) and the promise of Leviticus 26:42-45. The irony is in the book's own accusation that Israel broke the covenant (11:10; 31:32). In the new covenant of 31:31-34 the LORD himself promises a covenant 'not like' the broken one. The throne of his glory may be the Temple or the ark (3:16-17; 17:12).

p: Baal was the storm god of Canaan; the prayer says only the LORD gives rain.
b: In Canaanite belief, as the Ugaritic texts show, the storm god Baal gave rain and the fertility of the land. The prayer answers: the 'empty idols' (havlei hagoyim, the word of Ecclesiastes' hevel) cannot send rain, and the skies cannot give it on their own. The drought is therefore a contest: the people who turned to Baal for rain learn that rain is the LORD's to give or to hold, as in Elijah's time (1 Kings 17-18). The verdict on the myth is that the parallel is real: Israel's neighbors did credit their storm god, and the prophets argue directly against it.

p: Moses and Samuel stood in the gap for Israel; even they could not save this people.
b: Moses turned back the LORD's anger at the golden calf and at Kadesh (Exodus 32:11-14; Numbers 14:13-20; Psalm 106:23), and Samuel cried out for Israel at Mizpah (1 Samuel 7:8-9; 12:19-23). Psalm 99:6 joins them with Aaron among those who called on the LORD's name. Ezekiel 14:14 makes the same point with Noah, Daniel and Job. The saying does not say Moses and Samuel were weak; it says the sentence has been made. Jeremiah has already been banned from prayer (14:11) and now hears why it would not work. Moses and Samuel were dead by Jeremiah's day, which is why churches also ask here whether the saints pray for the living; that question is set out, with the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Reformed answers, in the card at Jeremiah 7:16 (the same topic, 'intercession').
r: Exodus 32:11-14; Numbers 14:13-20; 1 Samuel 7:8-9; 1 Samuel 12:19-23; Psalm 99:6; Ezekiel 14:14

a: Those meant for death, to death
p: Death, sword, famine, captivity: each person receives what they were marked for.
b: The four-fold verdict is repeated in 43:11 and Zechariah 11:9 uses a similar phrase. Revelation 13:10 reshapes it for the church: whoever is 'for captivity' goes into captivity, and whoever is to be killed by the sword will be killed by the sword. The first fate, mavet, is death by sickness or disease; the Plain English Translation treats it as 'death' because the next three are named separately.

p: Mishpachot means families or kinds; the four are sword, dogs, birds and animals.
b: The Hebrew word is mishpachot, 'families', used here for four 'kinds' or 'classes' of destroyers. The sword kills, dogs drag the bodies, and birds and beasts devour them: judgment moves from killing to the disgrace of no burial, which was a curse (Deuteronomy 28:26). Ezekiel 14:21 names four different 'severe judgments', and Leviticus 26:21-26 lists a similar sevenfold escalation. The Greek has 'I will take vengeance' (ekdikeso) where the Hebrew has 'I will appoint'.

p: Kings blames the exile on Manasseh; Jeremiah elsewhere blames the present generation.
b: Manasseh reigned fifty-five years and filled Jerusalem with idolatry and innocent blood (2 Kings 21:1-16), and 2 Kings 23:26-27 and 24:3-4 say the LORD did not turn from his anger, even after Josiah's reform, because of him. Jeremiah's other speeches charge the present generation with its own sins (16:12). Many critical scholars therefore see the mention of Manasseh in 15:4 as a later edit that brings Jeremiah in line with Kings (as Carroll and others argue); others hold that Jeremiah could say both, since nations suffer the results of earlier choices (compare Lamentations 5:7). The Greek has Manasseh here too. Ezekiel 18 and Jeremiah 31:29-30 insist each person bears his own guilt.
r: 2 Kings 21:10-15; 2 Kings 23:26-27; 2 Kings 24:3-4; Jeremiah 16:12; Jeremiah 31:29-30; Ezekiel 18:1-4

a: I am tired of changing my mind
p: Nicham: to change course out of pity; the LORD says he has run out of patience.
b: The verb nicham (also in 18:8, 10; 26:3, 13, 19) is the one used when God 'relents' or 'changes his mind' about a disaster he threatened (Exodus 32:14; Jonah 3:10). Here the LORD says he has grown tired of doing it. Jeremiah's hearers had been spared more than once (3:6-10), and the hope of repentance in chapters 3-4 and 18 is now gone. Other texts say God does not change his mind (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29); see the note on 18:8.

a: the mother of the young men
t: A mother, a young man, or both?
p: The Hebrew has 'mother of a young man'; the Greek has 'mother and young men'.
b: The Hebrew is 'em bachur, 'mother of a young man', which can be a collective 'mother of the young men' (the Plain English Translation) or mean 'mother [and] young man'. The Greek has 'against the mother, young men'. The picture is of mothers of soldiers, who lose their sons at noon, when armies did not attack: noon is the sign of a surprise (6:4; Zephaniah 2:4). Verse 9 then shows the mother of seven fainting.

p: Seven sons was the full measure of blessing; the mother is left with none.
b: Seven is the number of fullness. A mother of seven was the picture of blessing (1 Samuel 2:5; Ruth 4:15), and the picture of a woman 'whose sun has set at noon' comes from Amos 8:9. The image is bitter: the fullest blessing is now the fullest grief.

a: a man of strife and a man of contention
p: Five or six laments in which Jeremiah argues with God; scholars disagree about who is speaking.
b: The passages 11:18-12:6; 15:10-21; 17:12-18; 18:18-23; 20:7-18 are usually called Jeremiah's 'confessions'. Since Baumgartner's 1917 study they have been read as individual laments, like those of the Psalms. Views on the speaker differ: (1) Jeremiah himself, in prayers that record his inner life (the traditional view and that of Bright, Holladay and Lundbom); (2) a representative voice, a 'prophetic I' used in public worship (Reventlow), with the people or the faithful speaking through the prophet; (3) a literary creation by the book's editors to show the cost of a prophet's calling (Diamond reads them as part of the book's design). The Plain English Translation keeps them in the first person, as the Hebrew does.

p: Debt was the common cause of quarrels, so the saying means: I gave no one a reason to hate me.
b: Lending and borrowing were the usual cause of lawsuits and hatred (Proverbs 22:7; 2 Kings 4:1; Deuteronomy 24:10-13). Jeremiah says he is neither a lender nor a borrower, so there is nothing between him and anyone. His enemies curse him because of his word, not for any private quarrel.

a: Surely I will free you for good
p: The Hebrew is uncertain; it is an oath, and the Greek reads it as a prayer of Jeremiah.
b: The Hebrew opens with 'im lo, 'if not', the beginning of an oath ('surely'). The next word, written sharotikha and read sheritikha (the Masoretes' note), is of unknown meaning, taken as 'set free' (the Plain English Translation), 'strengthen' or 'serve you'. The verb paga' is 'to meet', and in the causative here, 'make [the enemy] meet [with you], make him plead'; it is also the verb of intercession. The Greek gives a quite different verse, a prayer of Jeremiah (see the variant). The Plain English Translation gives the LORD's promise that Jeremiah's enemies will in the end ask him for help, as Zedekiah does in 37:3 and 38:14-28.

p: A short riddle whose answer is the foe from the north; it may be misplaced.
b: 'Iron from the north' may mean the Babylonian army (the 'foe from the north' of chapters 4-6), whom no one can break; or the northern iron of the Chalybes, famous for its hardness; or it is a riddle whose answer is the LORD's word that Jeremiah is to be like iron (1:18; 15:20). The verse sits awkwardly between 15:11 and 15:13, and many scholars think it is out of place. Verses 13-14 are nearly the same as 17:3-4; the Greek lacks 17:1-4 but has 15:13-14. Which copy is the original is disputed.

a: Do not take me away by being slow to anger
p: Jeremiah fears God's patience with his enemies will cost him his life.
b: The Hebrew is 'do not, in the length of your anger, take me away'. 'Length of anger' ('erekh 'appayim) is the LORD's famous slowness to anger (Exodus 34:6). Jeremiah turns the creed against God: if you hold back your anger from them, they will kill me first. He takes his case to the God who 'knows' him (1:5), the same verb as at the start of the verse.

p: The scroll-eating of Ezekiel and Revelation has a model here.
b: Jeremiah eats the LORD's words as food, and they become joy. The picture is used again in Ezekiel 3:1-3 and Revelation 10:9-10, where the scroll is sweet as honey, and Deuteronomy 8:3 (quoted by Jesus in Matthew 4:4) says people live by every word from the LORD's mouth. Jeremiah's joy is also the source of his anguish: because he bears the LORD's name, he must bear the LORD's message (15:16-17).

a: the circle of those who make merry
p: A sod is a group of close companions; Jeremiah refuses the party.
b: The Hebrew sod is an inner circle of friends who sit together (Psalm 111:1; Job 15:8). Jeremiah withdraws from it because he is full of the LORD's anger (6:11). The command in chapter 16 not to enter a house of feasting or mourning is the public form of the same solitude: the prophet's life is a sign.

p: Achzav: a brook that flows in winter and is dry when needed.
b: Achzav comes from a root meaning 'to deceive, to fail'. The picture is of a winter stream-bed (a wadi) that runs when no one needs it and is dry in summer, like the brooks of Job 6:15-20 that disappoint travelers. Achzib in Micah 1:14 is a town whose name means 'deception'. The charge is shocking because the LORD calls himself 'the spring of living water' (2:13; 17:13), and Jeremiah accuses him of being the reverse. The accusation is not corrected; the LORD answers in the next verse.

a: If you turn back, I will turn you back
p: The verb shuv is used twice: if Jeremiah turns back, God will turn him back.
b: The LORD answers Jeremiah's complaint not with comfort but with a call to repent, using Jeremiah's own key verb in a pun: 'im tashuv va'ashivekha, 'if you return, I will return you'. He is told to bring out 'what is precious from what is worthless' (that is, to speak truly and not rant) and then to be 'like my mouth'; and the people will turn to him, not he to them. The prophet is not exempt from the message he brings. The command to turn is the same one he gave the people in 3:12-14, 22 and 8:4-5.

a: you will be like my mouth
t: The prophet as the LORD's mouth
p: The call of chapter 1 is renewed and tested.
b: In 1:9 the LORD touched Jeremiah's mouth and put his words in it; Exodus 4:16 and 7:1 already made Aaron and Moses a 'mouth' for the LORD. The new commission restates the old one after the prophet nearly gave up. The 'precious' and the 'worthless' (zolel, a rare word for cheap or vile things) are the prophet's own words and feelings: only what is pure may come out of his mouth.

a: a bronze wall with strong defenses
p: These two verses nearly repeat 1:18-19.
b: The promise that Jeremiah will be a wall of bronze that the people cannot overcome, because the LORD is with him to save him, is almost word for word 1:18-19. Placing it here, after the complaint, shows the LORD renewing his call. Whether the repetition is the editor's or Jeremiah's own recollection cannot be known.

p: Jeremiah's single life is a sign of the coming disaster, not a rule for others.
b: Hosea's marriage, Isaiah's naked walk and Ezekiel's wife's death (Hosea 1:2-9; Isaiah 20:2-4; Ezekiel 24:15-24) are signs given by the prophets' bodies and lives. Jeremiah's is that he may not marry or have children, for the children would die (16:3-4). Jews and Christians have not taken it as a rule for others: for Jews marriage and children were a command (Genesis 1:28), and the prophet's exception was part of the sign. Some Christian traditions, such as Catholic and Orthodox monastic life, honor celibacy for another reason, the kingdom of God (Matthew 19:12; 1 Corinthians 7:7-8, 26-29); Paul's 'present distress' (1 Corinthians 7:26) is the nearest NT parallel to Jeremiah's reason.

a: like dung on the surface of the ground
p: A corpse left unburied was the worst disgrace; Jeremiah repeats it for the dead of Jerusalem.
b: Burial in the family tomb was a duty and a comfort, and an unburied body was a curse (Deuteronomy 28:26; 1 Kings 14:11). Jeremiah says it of the people here and of the dead in 7:33 and 8:2; 25:33 and 22:19 say the same of King Jehoiakim. 'Dung' on the ground (also 8:2; 9:22; Psalm 83:10) is the picture of bodies that rot where they fall. The Greek has 'an example' (paradeigma) instead of dung.
r: Deuteronomy 28:26; 1 Kings 14:11; Jeremiah 7:33; Jeremiah 8:2; Jeremiah 22:19; Jeremiah 25:33

p: The Hebrew marzeach was a feasting group, with a meal and wine, known from Ugarit and Palmyra.
b: The Hebrew word is marzeach, which Amos 6:7 uses of a drinking feast of the rich. The same word is known from Ugaritic, Phoenician and Palmyrene texts as a society that met for a banquet, often tied to the dead. Here it seems to be a mourning meal, held at the house of the dead, where friends drank to comfort the family. The LORD forbids Jeremiah to join, because the LORD has withdrawn 'his peace, his loyal love, his compassion' from the people, so any comfort would be a lie.

a: cut himself, or shave his head
p: The law banned cutting and shaving for the dead, but the people did both.
b: Leviticus 19:28 and Deuteronomy 14:1 forbid gashing the body and shaving the front of the head for the dead, as the practice of other peoples. Jeremiah mentions them as normal (41:5; 47:5; 48:37), as do Isaiah 22:12 and Amos 8:10. The point here is that nothing will be done for the dead at all, neither the lawful signs of grief nor the banned ones.
r: Leviticus 19:28; Deuteronomy 14:1; Jeremiah 41:5; Jeremiah 47:5; Jeremiah 48:37; Isaiah 22:12

a: the sound of the groom and the sound of the bride
p: This line is repeated through the book and taken up again in Revelation.
b: The sounds of a wedding are the sign of an ordinary, living town. The Hebrew has qol, 'sound' or 'voice', each time: qol sason weqol simchah, qol chatan weqol kallah, and the Plain English Translation renders it 'sound' in all four places. Jeremiah says they will end (7:34; 16:9; 25:10) and will return (33:10-11). Revelation 18:23 uses the same words for the fall of Babylon the Great. Jeremiah is told not to marry, so he cannot hear them; his own household is silent, a sign to the town.

a: my law they did not keep
p: Here torah is the written law of the covenant; in 18:18 it is the priest's teaching.
b: The word torah means 'instruction', and the Plain English Translation renders it by context: 'law' where it is the commands of the covenant that the ancestors did not keep (here, 26:4; 32:23), 'teaching' where it is the instruction a priest gives (18:18). The verse also uses the standard language of Deuteronomy for idolatry: 'went after other gods, served them and bowed down to them' (Deuteronomy 8:19; 11:16; 29:26). Critical scholars call this the 'Deuteronomistic prose' style of the book's sermons; traditional readers hold that Jeremiah himself absorbed Deuteronomy's language after Josiah's reform.

a: I will give you no favor
p: The word chaninah appears only here: the other gods will show no favor either.
b: The noun chaninah, 'favor, grace', is found only here in the Bible. The sentence turns on irony: those who wanted other gods' favor will serve them 'day and night' and receive none, since the LORD gives none and the other gods have none to give. It is the cruelest line of the speech.

a: it will no longer be said
p: The oath 'as the LORD lives who brought us out of Egypt' will be replaced by a greater one.
b: The Exodus was Israel's founding act, and people swore by it. Jeremiah promises a return from 'the land of the north' that will be so great it will replace the Exodus in their oaths. The same promise is made nearly word for word in 23:7-8 (where the Greek has it in the same place). Isaiah 43:16-19 and 48:20-21 also promise a new exodus. Note the sequence: this promise stands right after the worst judgment, and 'the land of the north', which was the home of the foe in chapters 4-6, is now where the exiles live.

t: Fishers and hunters: rescue or judgment?
p: The image can mean enemies who capture or messengers who gather.
b: The context is the exile: the LORD sends 'fishermen' and 'hunters' after the people, to drag them from hiding places. Other prophets use fishing for judgment (Amos 4:2; Habakkuk 1:14-17; Ezekiel 29:4), which fits the second half of the verse with its hunters in the rock clefts. Some readers take the fishermen as gatherers who bring the people home, after the promise of verse 15. Christian readers have also seen Jesus' call to 'fishers of people' (Mark 1:17) in the image, though Mark's wording is his own. The Plain English Translation keeps the order the Hebrew has: fishermen first, then hunters.

p: Mishneh may mean 'double' or 'the full equivalent'.
b: Mishneh is 'a second, a double'. It can mean twice the debt, as in the stolen-goods law (Exodus 22:4, 7, 9), or a full equal repayment (compare Isaiah 40:2). In either sense, it is the price of defiling the land with the corpses of idols, which here means the lifeless images and perhaps the sacrifices to them.

t: The nations turn to the LORD
p: A rare hopeful word for the nations in a judgment chapter.
b: In the middle of a sentence of judgment, Jeremiah looks beyond it: the nations will come to the LORD and say that their ancestors' gods were nothing. The same hope is in 3:17; 12:15-16; Isaiah 2:2-4 and Zechariah 8:20-23. The idols are called sheqer and hevel, 'falsehood' and 'emptiness', the book's two words for them. Verse 21 then says that the LORD will make his people know his name.

p: The aim of the judgment is the knowledge that he is the LORD.
b: 'They will know that my name is the LORD' is the goal of the Exodus (Exodus 6:3, 7; 7:5) and of Ezekiel's repeated 'they will know that I am the LORD'. Here the 'hand' and 'might' are those of the Exodus (Deuteronomy 3:24). The judgment, as bitter as it is, is meant to teach.

t: Written with iron, engraved on the heart
p: Judah's sin is carved in permanent letters on the heart and on the altar.
b: The iron pen and the point of flint (or diamond: shamir is a very hard stone) are tools for cutting stone, as in Job 19:24, where Job wishes his words were cut in rock. Here the sin is cut into 'the tablet of their heart', the very place where the LORD will write his teaching in the new covenant (31:33; compare Proverbs 3:3; 7:3), and into the horns of the altars, where the blood of the sin offering was meant to be put to cover sin (Leviticus 4:7, 18, 25, 30). The altars that should have cleansed record the guilt. The Greek lacks 17:1-4 (see the variant).

p: Asherah was a goddess, and her wooden pole stood beside altars until Josiah cut them down.
b: Asherah (plural 'asherim, as here) names a Canaanite goddess and also the wooden pole or tree set up for her near an altar (Deuteronomy 16:21; 1 Kings 15:13; 2 Kings 21:7). Josiah burned Asherah's pole and tore down the houses where women wove for her (2 Kings 23:4-7). Whether a goddess named Asherah was ever honored as the LORD's consort is debated in light of inscriptions at Kuntillet 'Ajrud that mention 'the LORD of Samaria and his asherah', a reading that remains disputed. Jeremiah's point is plain: the children inherit the altars their parents built.

p: The verb is the one for the sabbatical release; the land will have its rest.
b: The verb shamat is the one for 'releasing' land in the seventh year (Exodus 23:11) and debts (Deuteronomy 15:1-2). Judah will 'release' its inheritance, though not as a pious act: by its own doing it will lose the land. Leviticus 26:34-35 said the land would enjoy its sabbaths while the people were in exile, and 2 Chronicles 36:21 links this to Jeremiah's seventy years. A reader who knows the Sabbath law (17:19-27) sees the connection: a people that would not keep sabbaths will give the land its sabbaths.

a: Cursed is the one who trusts in humankind
t: Trust in humans or in the LORD
p: The curse and the blessing are the two ways of Deuteronomy and Psalm 1.
b: The poem sets two trusts side by side: the person who trusts in humans and makes 'flesh' his strength, and the person who trusts in the LORD. 'Flesh' (basar) is human weakness, as in Isaiah 31:3 (Egypt's horses are 'flesh, not spirit') and Psalm 146:3. The context in Jeremiah is the political trust in Egypt and in alliances (2:36-37). The pair of curse and blessing is the form of Deuteronomy 27-28 and of the 'two ways' (Psalm 1; Deuteronomy 30:15-19).

p: The tree by the water is also in Psalm 1; which came first is debated.
b: Psalm 1:3 describes the one who delights in the LORD's teaching as 'a tree planted by streams of water' whose leaf does not wither and who bears fruit in season. Jeremiah's version is a poem on trust, with the shrub in the salt desert as its opposite. The relation of the two is disputed: Jeremiah may have used a wisdom saying that Psalm 1 also knows, Psalm 1 may have borrowed from Jeremiah, or Jeremiah from an earlier psalm. Neither dependence is certain. The common image makes them companion pieces: the trusting person is rooted where water is.

t: The heart: deceitful, or just crooked?
p: The line is often quoted as proof of human depravity; the Hebrew is blunter and narrower.
b: 'Aqov comes from the root of ya'aqov, 'Jacob' (the heel-grabber), and means 'crooked, tricky'. 'Anush is used of an incurable wound or sickness (15:18; 30:12, 15) and in the KJV became 'desperately wicked', which says more than the Hebrew does. The Greek reads quite differently ('deep' and 'it is man'), see the variants. Church teaching has used the verse for human sinfulness in general, but the context speaks of Judah's heart and the sin engraved on it (17:1, 9), and the book also says the LORD will give a new heart (24:7; 31:33). The question 'Who can know it?' is answered at once: 'I, the LORD, search the heart.'
r: Jeremiah 15:18; Jeremiah 24:7; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26; Genesis 6:5; Mark 7:21-23

p: The kidneys were the seat of the deepest feelings; Christ speaks these words in Revelation.
b: The Hebrew kelayot, 'kidneys', stands for the hidden inner life (11:20; 12:2; Psalm 7:9; 26:2), the KJV 'reins'. 'Fruit of his deeds' continues the tree image of verse 8. In Revelation 2:23 the risen Christ says he is the one who 'searches minds and hearts' and repays each according to his deeds, taking the LORD's words in Jeremiah 17:10 for himself.

a: a partridge that gathers a brood
p: The partridge was thought to hatch eggs it had not laid.
b: The proverb says a partridge gathers a brood it did not lay. Whether the bird really does so, or whether this was only an ancient belief, is uncertain; the proverb works if the hearers believed it. The one who makes wealth unjustly will see it 'leave him', as the chicks leave the stranger-mother, in the middle of his days. The 'fool' (naval) is the one who ignores God, as in Psalm 14:1.

p: Jeremiah's title for the LORD, taken up by Jesus.
b: The LORD is 'the spring of living water' here and in 2:13, which also speaks of the broken cisterns. The word miqveh, 'hope', also means a gathering of water (see the note on 14:8), so 'hope of Israel' and 'spring' meet. Jesus uses the same image of himself in John 4:10-14 and 7:37-38, and Revelation 7:17 and 21:6 apply it to the water of life. 'Living' water is moving water, as opposed to the standing water of a cistern.

a: Those who turn away from me will be written in the earth
p: Names written in dust are soon gone; a speaker shift makes the line odd.
b: The Masoretic Text gives the speaker as 'me' while the rest of the verse talks to 'you': so the Plain English Translation keeps 'from me' and flags the shift. The Masoretic pointing is yesurai, 'those who turn away from me'; the Ketiv data in the ETCBC texts records the written form as yisorai, a different vowel pattern of the same root (see the variant). The Greek has 'those who stand away on the earth'. To be 'written in the earth' is to have a name that will not last, the opposite of a name in the book of life (Exodus 32:32-33; Daniel 12:1). Commentators often compare Jesus, who wrote on the ground while the accusers stood before him (John 8:6, 8), though John does not quote this verse.

a: Heal me, LORD, and I will be healed
p: Healing is the LORD's own title and Israel's hope.
b: The prayer is built on the verb rafa'. The LORD calls himself Israel's healer in Exodus 15:26, and Jeremiah's people ask in 14:19 why they cannot be healed. The LORD promises to heal the 'turnings away' in 3:22 and 30:17, so the confession ends with a plea whose answer the book keeps for chapters 30-33. 'You are my praise' means: you are what I praise, and the cause of my praising.

a: Where is the word of the LORD?
p: The test of Deuteronomy 18:22 is thrown back at Jeremiah.
b: The people say, in effect, 'Where is the word you promised?' This is the taunt of Isaiah 5:19 and Ezekiel 12:22, 27, and in the New Testament 2 Peter 3:4 speaks of those who ask where the promised coming is. Deuteronomy 18:22 said the test of a prophet is whether his word comes true. Jeremiah's reply is not to defend himself with a sign but to say he did not hurry the disaster (verse 16).

p: The text is uncertain: 'from being a shepherd', 'from evil', or a Greek reading 'I did not grow tired'.
b: The Hebrew says mero'eh 'acharekha, 'from shepherding after you'. The prophet may call himself a shepherd who follows the LORD the shepherd, and has not run from the job. Some emend ro'eh to ra'ah, 'from evil', giving 'I have not pressed you for disaster'; the Greek says 'I did not grow weary following after you'. The Plain English Translation keeps the Masoretic word and the sense that Jeremiah did not wish for the people's ruin (compare 18:20).

p: The Hebrew is 'Gate of the sons of the people'; its place is not known.
b: The name is sha'ar bene ha'am, 'the gate of the sons of the people' (the written text, the Ketiv, lacks the article on 'people', and so does the scroll 4QJer-a; the Greek has 'the gates of the sons of your people'). No other text names it. Its place is unknown. Jeremiah is to stand there and in 'all the gates', so the sermon is meant to reach everyone who comes and goes, king and common person alike.

a: Do not haul a load on the sabbath day
p: The Torah does not forbid carrying by name; Jeremiah, Nehemiah and the rabbis take it up.
b: The Ten Commandments forbid 'work' on the sabbath without listing it (Exodus 20:8-11). This passage names one case: carrying burdens to market through the gates. Amos 8:5 shows merchants impatient for the sabbath to end. After the exile Nehemiah closed the gates on sabbath for the same reason (Nehemiah 13:15-22). The rabbis list carrying from one domain to another among the thirty-nine kinds of work (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2). That rabbinic law is later than Jeremiah and has its own reasoning; this passage is the best-known earlier text naming carrying on the sabbath. The principle for Jeremiah is that the sabbath is a gift of rest for everyone, from the king to the common person (17:25-26), and that its neglect was a mark of a people who had no ear for the LORD.

p: A stubborn ox that will not be led.
b: To 'stiffen the neck' (qishu 'oref) is the image of an ox that will not take the yoke. It is Exodus 32:9's charge against Israel at the golden calf, repeated in 7:26 and 19:15. The Greek adds 'more than their fathers'.

a: kings and princes who sit on David's throne
p: The promise to David's line is tied to keeping the sabbath.
b: The blessing offered here is the one Jeremiah elsewhere ties to justice (22:1-5): if the kings obey, the dynasty will continue. The promise to David in 2 Samuel 7:12-16 is unconditional in that text, but Psalm 132:12 and 1 Kings 2:4 make the sons' faithfulness a condition. This is one of the book's conditional offers, like 18:7-10. See also the note on 17:27.

a: I will kindle a fire in its gates
p: The sermon ends with the same threat as Amos' sermons against the nations.
b: Fire on the fortresses ('armenot) is the formula of Amos 1-2, in which the LORD sends fire against the strongholds of nations and of Judah (Amos 2:5). Jeremiah 21:14; 43:12 and 49:27 use it too. The threat came true in 586 BC, when the city gates and Temple burned (39:8; 52:13). The conditional form 'if you ... but if you do not' is that of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28.

p: The Hebrew says 'on the two stones': a pair of discs, the lower turned by the foot.
b: The Hebrew 'al ha'ovnayim means 'on the two stones', the two discs of a potter's wheel, a heavy lower one that is turned and an upper one on which the clay sits. Ben Sira describes a potter at his wheel, turning it with his feet (Sirach 38:29-30). Potters worked in a quarter of Jerusalem, near the Potsherd Gate (19:2). The picture in 18:4 is of a shape that collapses and is simply reworked while the clay is still wet.

t: The same verb as the loincloth
p: Shachat, 'ruin', is the verb of the loincloth in chapter 13.
b: The verb shachat is used for the loincloth 'ruined' in 13:7 and the LORD's promise to 'ruin' Judah's pride in 13:9. Here the vessel is 'ruined' in the potter's hand, but the potter is not defeated: he shapes another. The contrast with chapter 13 is deliberate: the loincloth could not be mended, while clay can be reshaped. See 19:11, where the clay has been fired and cannot be.

a: Am I unable to treat you
p: Isaiah, Sirach, Wisdom and Paul use the same picture, and it is used differently in each.
b: The LORD as potter and Israel as clay appears in Isaiah 29:16; 45:9 and 64:8, and in Sirach 36:13. In Isaiah 45:9 it rebukes those who argue with their maker. Jeremiah's use is its own: the potter's freedom includes the freedom to reshape a spoiled vessel, and the rest of the passage (18:7-10) says the LORD's plan for a nation depends on how the nation answers. Paul takes the picture in Romans 9:20-21 for God's right over the clay; the link to Jeremiah 18 is possible, but commentators usually think he is drawing on Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9 (Wisdom 15:7 is another potter text often read beside Romans 9). See the card below on predestination.

a: pull it up, pull it down and destroy it
p: The verbs of 1:10 return here, with their conditions.
b: These verbs, 'pluck up, pull down, destroy', and the pair 'build and plant' of verse 9, are those of Jeremiah's commission in 1:10, where he is set over nations. The principle is spelled out here: the LORD's word against or for a nation is not a fixed sentence. It is open to the nation's response, as the example of Nineveh shows (Jonah 3:10). The lesson is repeated in 26:3, 13 and 42:10 and is Jeremiah's reply to the idea that prophecy is a prediction.

a: I will change my mind about the harm
p: Jeremiah 18 has the LORD relent; other texts say he does not. Traditions have read this differently.
b: The verb is nicham (see 15:6); the same word, ra'ah, is used for the nation's wickedness and for the harm the LORD planned. Jeremiah 18:7-10, 26:3, Exodus 32:14 and Jonah 3:10 show God changing course; Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 say he is not a human who 'relents'. Classic teaching, as in Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I, q. 19, a. 7), holds that God's will does not change and that texts about his 'relenting' describe our experience of an unchanging God. Calvin says the same by way of 'accommodation' (Institutes 1.17.12-13). Others, such as Fretheim, argue that the texts show a real responsiveness in God, who will genuinely change plans when people change. The Jewish reading is that the decree is always conditional on repentance, as in Jonah.

a: does what is evil in my eyes
p: Ra'ah is the nation's evil and the LORD's disaster.
b: In 18:8 the nation turns from its ra'ah (wickedness) and the LORD changes his mind about the ra'ah (harm) he planned; here the nation does what is ra' (evil) and the LORD changes his mind about the tov, the good. The Plain English Translation uses 'wickedness' and 'harm' in verse 8 (as 26:3 does) and 'evil' here, but the repeated Hebrew word is what makes the passage hang together: evil done and evil sent are linked by the same word.

p: Yotser 'potter' and yatsar 'shape': the LORD is shaping disaster as a potter shapes clay.
b: The word for 'potter' is yotser, and the verb here, 'I am shaping' (yotser), is the same, so the line says literally 'I am a potter, potting disaster against you'. English can say 'shaping'. The plan (machashavah) against Judah is still being made and can still be changed by a turn: 'Turn back, each of you.' Isaiah 45:7 uses the verb for God forming light and disaster.

p: The people's answer is a single word, no'ash, 'it is hopeless'.
b: No'ash is 'it is hopeless, there is no point'. They had said it before (2:25) about turning back from their lovers. After a chapter that offered a way out, their reply is a shrug. Their line, 'We will follow our own plans', answers God's 'plan' with their own.

p: Betulat Yisra'el: a title of affection that turns up again in the Book of Consolation.
b: The same title, 'the virgin Israel', is a term of tenderness: the LORD will rebuild her in 31:4 and 31:21. Here she has done a horrible thing: the people have been unfaithful to a faithful God. The nations are the witnesses, as in 2:10-11, where the question 'has a nation changed its gods?' makes the same point.

a: the rock of the open country
p: The Hebrew is obscure; the Greek reads it quite differently.
b: The meaning is that nature is reliable (snow stays on Lebanon, cold water keeps flowing) and God's people are not. The words themselves are unclear: tsur sadai could be 'the rock of the open country' (the Plain English Translation), 'the rocky height of Sirion' or a different division of the consonants. The Greek says 'Will breasts fail from a rock?', reading shadai as 'breasts'. The Plain English Translation gives the sense the context needs, and flags it as uncertain.

a: on the paths of long ago
p: In 6:16 the LORD told them to ask for the ancient paths; here they are left.
b: Jeremiah 6:16 told the people to ask for 'the ancient paths' and find the good way; they said 'We will not walk in it.' Here they have been made to stumble on the very paths of antiquity and take side paths on 'a road not built up', a track without a prepared bed. It is the image of a nation off the road, in the wilderness that the same chapter's 'ruin' predicts.

p: Sheriqah: a sound of scorn at a ruined place.
b: Sheriqot (the Masoretes' reading; the written word is sheruqat) is a whistle or hiss of scorn and shock, the sound passers-by make at a ruin. Jeremiah uses it often (19:8; 25:9, 18; 29:18; 49:17; 50:13; 51:37), as do 1 Kings 9:8 and Lamentations 2:15-16. Shaking the head is the same gesture of horror.

p: To show the back is to hide the face.
b: To turn the back is the opposite of the priestly blessing, 'May the LORD make his face shine on you' (Numbers 6:25). In 2:27 the people 'turned their backs, not their faces' to the LORD; here the LORD does the same to them. Moses saw only the LORD's back (Exodus 33:23), so seeing the back can also mean something like a partial vision; here the sense is only absence.

a: teaching will not be lost from the priest
p: The enemies name the priest's teaching, the sage's advice and the prophet's word.
b: Priest, wise man and prophet are the three recognized guides, each with a gift: torah (the Plain English Translation says 'teaching', since a priest gives instruction on what is clean and what is not), 'etsah (advice) and davar (word). Ezekiel 7:26 has the same three; Jeremiah 8:8-9 and 2:8 contest each of them. The plotters argue that the community has enough guidance without Jeremiah. The Qumran copy 4QJer-a preserves this verse and agrees with the Masoretic Text on the main words. The Greek has 'law' (nomos).

a: Is good paid back with evil?
p: The same complaint in the Psalms of David.
b: The complaint 'they repay me evil for good' is that of Psalm 35:12 and 109:4-5, and the pit dug for the faithful is that of Psalm 57:6; compare also Proverbs 17:13. Jeremiah's claim that he stood before God to speak good for them and turn away his anger fits 14:7-9, 19-22, where he did pray for them. The demand in verses 21-23 follows from that betrayal.

a: So hand their sons over to hunger
p: Jeremiah asks for terrible things; readers disagree about what to make of it.
b: This is the harshest of the confessions, and it is no accident that it comes right after the report of the plot. Readers divide: (1) it is an honest cry of a man in danger, presented in scripture as a prayer, not an example; the prophet leaves vengeance to God, the position of Romans 12:19; (2) it fits the covenant curses the prophet has himself announced, so he is only asking the LORD to do what he has said he will do; (3) Christian readers who recall Jesus' command to love enemies (Matthew 5:44; Luke 23:34) usually say such prayers are not for Christians to copy; they are still scripture because they show what a believer may bring to God. The word 'pour' (hagerem) is literally 'pour them out' on the power of the sword.

a: Do not make atonement for their guilt
p: Kipper 'cover over, make atonement' is used for forgiving, so the prayer asks that guilt not be forgiven.
b: The verb is kipper (see the Plain English Translation's term 'make atonement'); with 'al and 'iniquity' it means to cover a sin over so that it is forgiven. The prayer asks the opposite, that the LORD not forgive them. Nehemiah 4:5 uses the same words in a similar prayer. The Qumran copy 4QJer-a seems to repeat the phrase 'on their guilt' twice (a doubled phrase, probably a scribe's slip) and otherwise agrees with the Masoretic Text.

p: A baqbuq was a narrow-necked flask, named for the sound it made when emptied.
b: The Hebrew baqbuq is a flask or jug with a narrow neck, the word imitating the gurgle of liquid poured out. In 1 Kings 14:3 it holds a gift of honey. The purchase in the potter's shop follows the visit of chapter 18: a ready-made, fired vessel, bought and carried to the Potsherd Gate, where it will be smashed. The elders whom Jeremiah takes are the witnesses of the sign.

p: The gate opened on the Valley of Hinnom where pottery was dumped.
b: Charsit comes from cheres, 'potsherd, broken pottery', and the name is probably from the heaps of broken pots. It is the only mention of the gate. The Greek has a transliteration (Tharseis) and calls the valley a 'burial ground' (polyandrion).

p: The valley south of Jerusalem became the name of the place of fire, Gehenna.
b: The Valley of Ben-hinnom ('son of Hinnom') runs along the south and west of old Jerusalem (Joshua 15:8). Manasseh and Ahaz burned sons there (2 Chronicles 28:3; 33:6), and Josiah defiled it (2 Kings 23:10). Jeremiah calls it a valley of slaughter. In the centuries before Jesus, writers used 'Gehenna' (Hebrew ge-hinnom) for the place where the wicked would be punished (1 Enoch 27; 90:26). Jesus speaks of Gehenna (Matthew 5:22, 29-30; 10:28; Mark 9:43-48), and 'hell' in many English Bibles translates that name. The nt-lane topic 'gehenna' follows that story.
r: Joshua 15:8; 2 Kings 23:10; 2 Chronicles 28:3; Jeremiah 7:31-32; Matthew 5:22; Mark 9:43-48; 1 Enoch 27

a: burn their children in the fire
p: The Bible says children were burned in the valley; the word, the god and the practice are still debated.
b: Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2-5 forbid giving a child 'to Molech'; 2 Kings 23:10 says Josiah defiled the Topheth so no one could pass a son or daughter through the fire; Jeremiah 7:31 and 32:35 describe it. Here the god is Baal; in 32:35 it is Molech (the two may be one cult, or the writers name the god differently). Some scholars have argued that 'passing through the fire' meant a dedication ritual in which children lived, but Jeremiah's language ('burn', 'burnt offerings') and Ezekiel 16:21; 23:39 say the children died. In Carthage, burial grounds of burned infants called 'tophets' hold urns; whether they show sacrifice or the cremation of children who died young is still argued.
r: Leviticus 18:21; Leviticus 20:2-5; 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31; Jeremiah 32:35; Ezekiel 16:21

p: The LORD denies that he ever asked for child sacrifice; Ezekiel and Exodus raise a question.
b: Jeremiah repeats the denial in 7:31 and 32:35. The Greek of this verse lacks 'I never spoke of it'. The need to say it suggests some thought the LORD wanted it. Exodus 22:29 says 'the firstborn of your sons you shall give to me' (the law then provides redemption in Exodus 13:13), and Ezekiel 20:25-26 says the LORD gave Israel 'statutes that were not good' and polluted them through their gifts of the firstborn. Readers take that in different ways: as a harsh judgment on a people who misused the firstborn law, or as an ironic description of how their own acts became the verdict. Jeremiah's answer is flat: it never entered the LORD's mind.

p: The meaning of 'Topheth' is unknown; a common suggestion is that its vowels are those of boshet, 'shame'.
b: No one is sure what topheth means. It may come from an Aramaic word for 'hearth' or 'fire-place', or may be a word for a burning place. A common suggestion is that the Masoretes gave it the vowels of bosheth, 'shame' (the word that replaced 'Baal' in some names), so as not to say the original name aloud. Isaiah 30:33 has a 'Topheth' for the fire prepared for the king of Assyria. Jeremiah promises that its name will change to 'the Valley of Slaughter', a name for what it will become.

t: Baqoti: the jar word in the verb
p: The verb 'empty out' (baqoti) sounds like baqbuq, the jar.
b: The verb baqoti ('I will empty out, make void') is built from the same letters and sound as baqbuq, 'jar', which the prophet is carrying. The jar that gurgles as it empties is the sign of the plans of Judah emptied out. English cannot keep the sound, so 'empty out' and 'jar' have to do. Compare Isaiah 19:3 and 24:1, 3, where the same verb is used for emptying a land.

a: their own sons' flesh and their daughters' flesh
p: A covenant curse that was carried out during sieges.
b: Eating one's children is the extreme covenant curse of Leviticus 26:29 and Deuteronomy 28:53-57, and happened in the siege of Samaria (2 Kings 6:28-29), in Jerusalem in 586 BC (Lamentations 2:20; 4:10; Ezekiel 5:10), and, Josephus reports, in the siege of AD 70 (Jewish War 6.3.4). Jeremiah uses it as a sign of how far the 'distress' of siege will go.

a: a potter's vessel that cannot be made whole again
p: In chapter 18 a flawed pot is remade; here a baked pot is smashed past mending.
b: The two potter signs are meant to be read together. In 18:4 the clay is still soft and the potter simply reshapes it, which is the picture of a God who will change his mind if the people turn. In 19:10-11 the jar is baked hard and, once broken, 'cannot be repaired'. Some readers see a change in time: the offer of 18:7-10 was open, but is now closed; others see two aspects of one God. The jar's destruction does not mean that the clay is thrown away forever: 18:4 and 24:6 and 31:4 speak of rebuilding.

p: Sun, moon and stars were worshiped on flat house roofs; Josiah had removed such altars.
b: 'The host of heaven' means the sun, moon and stars, whose worship Deuteronomy 4:19 forbids. Houses had flat roofs, and altars on them are mentioned in 2 Kings 23:12 (Josiah smashed 'the altars on the roof of the upper room of Ahaz'), Zephaniah 1:5 and Jeremiah 32:29. It leads to the Queen of Heaven in 7:18 and 44:17-25.
r: Deuteronomy 4:19; 2 Kings 23:12; Zephaniah 1:5; Jeremiah 7:18; Jeremiah 32:29; Jeremiah 44:17-25

p: Pashhur was a priest of the house of Immer and the Temple's chief officer.
b: Pashhur's title (paqid nagid) is 'officer, leader': he was in charge of order in the Temple area, a role like that of the 'overseer' Zephaniah in 29:25-26. The priestly house of Immer is one of the twenty-four courses (1 Chronicles 24:14), and Immer's family returned from exile (Ezra 2:37). He is not Pashhur son of Malchijah (21:1; 38:1), and not the Pashhur whose son Gedaliah appears in 38:1.

p: A device that twisted the body; also in 29:26 and 2 Chronicles 16:10.
b: The mahpekhet ('twister', from hafakh, 'turn') held the prisoner's body bent. Jeremiah 29:26 says every madman who prophesies is to be put in stocks and collar. In 2 Chronicles 16:10 Asa puts the seer Hanani in the 'house of the stocks'. The Upper Gate of Benjamin was an entrance of the Temple area (Ezekiel 9:2 speaks of the upper gate).

a: The LORD has not called your name Pashhur
p: Magor missaviv, 'Terror all around', was Jeremiah's catchphrase, and now Pashhur's new name.
b: Magor missaviv is a phrase Jeremiah used often (6:25; 20:10; 46:5; 49:29), and it appears in Psalm 31:13 and Lamentations 2:22. His enemies throw it back in 20:10. Here he gives it to Pashhur as a new name: Pashhur will himself be the terror. Pashhur may be an Egyptian name meaning 'son of Horus', which was in use in priestly families. Name changes in prophets are signs (Isaiah 8:3; Hosea 1:6-9). The Greek has 'Exile' here (see the variant).
r: Jeremiah 6:25; Jeremiah 20:10; Jeremiah 46:5; Jeremiah 49:29; Psalm 31:13; Isaiah 8:3

t: The first time Babylon is named
p: The foe from the north of chapters 4-6 gets a name here.
b: In the order of the book this is the first place where the LORD names Babylon as the power that will do it. Chapters 4-6 spoke of an unnamed foe from the north, which some have identified with the Scythians (Herodotus, Histories 1.103-106, tells of a Scythian raid; the view is now less favored) and most now identify with Babylon. Babylon became the great power after Nebuchadnezzar's victory at Carchemish in 605 BC, which the Babylonian Chronicle records. Pashhur's oracle is usually put in Jehoiakim's reign, between 605 and 598 BC.

a: You enticed me, LORD, and I was enticed
p: The verb pittah ranges from 'persuade' to 'seduce'; English has usually said 'deceived'.
b: The verb pittah means to persuade or entice, and is used for the seducing of a young woman (Exodus 22:16), for Delilah's coaxing of Samson (Judges 16:5), and for the LORD's 'enticing' Ahab through a lying spirit (1 Kings 22:20-22) and a prophet through his own words (Ezekiel 14:9). The Greek (ēpatēsas, 'you deceived') and the older English versions, which sit between it and the Latin seduxisti, read 'deceived'. Rashi takes it as 'You enticed me to go on your mission' and glosses 'you were stronger' as 'you overcame me against my will' (as given in the Sefaria text). Some modern interpreters hear the language of seduction and force (compare Deuteronomy 22:25-28 for the pair 'entice' and 'seize'), others reject that as too strong. The Plain English Translation keeps 'entice' so that 20:10, where Jeremiah's enemies hope he will be 'enticed', uses the same word. Jeremiah's cry is a charge against the LORD, who answers it nowhere.

p: The two words he must cry are the same as in 6:7.
b: Chamas vashod, 'violence and destruction', is the cry of 6:7, and Habakkuk 1:2-3 shows another prophet using the same words. Jeremiah's message is one word of doom, so his hearers laugh. The cry is also what a victim shouts for help: it is possible the Hebrew leaves both ideas open.

t: A fire he cannot hold in
p: Prophets elsewhere speak of the same compulsion.
b: The compulsion of the word is described in Amos 3:8 ('The LORD has spoken; who can but prophesy?'), Job 32:18-20, and by Paul in 1 Corinthians 9:16. Psalm 39:1-3 has a psalmist whose silence made a fire burn in him. For Jeremiah, to stop speaking is not possible, even though speaking has cost him everything. The Qumran copy 4QJer-c preserves the verse and agrees with the Masoretic text in these words.

p: His enemies hope Jeremiah will be 'enticed', as he said the LORD enticed him.
b: The enemies use the verb of 20:7, yefutteh, and so make Jeremiah's complaint against God the very plan of men: they will trap him as he says God did. The Plain English Translation repeats 'enticed' to keep the echo. 'Terror all around' here is their quotation of his own words (see 20:3). 'Report him!' is an informer's call (Psalm 31:13 has the same pairing of terror and whispers).

a: You see the kidneys and the heart
p: These lines repeat Jeremiah 11:20 nearly word for word.
b: Jeremiah 11:20 (the first confession) has almost the same words, and 17:10 says it of the LORD speaking. Placing the line at the start and the end of the confessions frames them. The Greek has 'testing righteous things' for 'testing the righteous'.

t: A hymn in the middle of a curse
p: The praise seems to jump out of nowhere between two cries of despair.
b: Verse 13 is a short hymn of the kind found in the Psalms, placed between the complaint and the curse of the day of birth. Readers take it differently: as a lament form that includes a vow of praise, which is then overturned by what follows; as a fragment moved here by editors; or as Jeremiah's real moment of confidence before the dark. 4QJer-c preserves the whole verse and 4QJer-a its last line, both agreeing with the Masoretic Text, and the Greek has it, so it was in the Hebrew of both editions. The Plain English Translation does not decide what the sequence means. The reader is left, as the book leaves Jeremiah, without resolution.

t: The curse of the day of birth
p: The same curse is in Job 3, and Jeremiah's own call said the LORD knew him before birth.
b: Cursing the day of one's birth is also the opening of Job 3:1-10, where it is spoken by Job in his suffering; which text depends on the other is debated, and some find a shared tradition. Jeremiah's version is tied to his own story: the LORD had told him he was known and set apart before he was formed (1:5), and now he wishes the womb had been his grave. The words are among the bleakest of the Bible. The book does not answer; Jeremiah does not curse God, only the day.

a: the LORD overturned without changing his mind
p: The cities are Sodom and Gomorrah, the standard overthrown cities.
b: The cities the LORD 'overthrew' are Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24-25; Deuteronomy 29:23; Amos 4:11), and Jeremiah uses them again for Edom (49:18) and Babylon (50:40). The Hebrew says the LORD overturned them 'and did not relent', using the verb nicham of 15:6 and 18:8: this time there is no relenting. The man who brought the news is cursed with the cry and war-shout of a city under attack. The curse is rhetorical; the messenger is a figure, not a real person who can be blamed.
